{{Short description|Subgroup mapped to itself under every automorphism of the parent group}}

{{more footnotes|date=August 2026}}

In [[group theory]], a '''characteristic subgroup''' is a [[subgroup]] that is mapped to itself by every [[automorphism]] of the parent [[group (mathematics)|group]].{{sfnp|Dummit|Foote|2003|p=135}}{{sfnp|Lang|2002}} Because every [[Conjugacy class#Properties|conjugation map]] is an [[inner automorphism]], every characteristic subgroup is [[normal subgroup|normal]]; though the converse is not true. Examples of characteristic subgroups include the [[commutator subgroup]] and the [[center of a group]].

== Definition ==
A subgroup <math>H</math> of a group <math>G</math> is called a '''characteristic subgroup''' if for every automorphism <math>\varphi</math> of <math>G</math>, one has <math>\varphi(H)\leq H</math>; then write '''{{math|''H'' char ''G''}}'''.

This is equivalent to the stronger condition <math>\varphi(H) = H</math> for every automorphism <math>\varphi</math> of <math>G</math>, because <math>\varphi^{-1}(H)\leq H</math> implies the reverse inclusion <math>H\leq \varphi(H)</math>.

== Basic properties ==

Given <math>H\,\mathrm{char}\,G</math>, every automorphism of <math>G</math> induces an automorphism of the [[quotient group]] <math>G/H</math>, which yields a homomorphism <math>\operatorname{Aut}(G)\to\operatorname{Aut}(G/H)</math>.

If <math>G</math> has a unique subgroup <math>H</math> of a given [[index of a subgroup|index]], then <math>H</math> is characteristic in <math>G</math>.

== Related concepts ==

=== Normal subgroup ===
{{main|Normal subgroup}}
A subgroup <math>H</math> of <math>G</math> that is invariant under all inner automorphisms is called [[normal subgroup|normal]]; sometimes called an invariant subgroup.

Since <math>\operatorname{Inn}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{Aut}(G)</math> and a characteristic subgroup is invariant under all automorphisms, every characteristic subgroup is normal. However, not every normal subgroup is characteristic. Here are several examples:
* Let <math>H</math> be a nontrivial group, and let <math>G=H\times H</math> be the [[direct product of groups|direct product]]. Then the subgroups <math>\{1\}\times H</math> and <math>H\times \{1\}</math> are both normal, but neither is characteristic. In particular, neither of these subgroups is invariant under the automorphism <math>(x,y)\mapsto (y,x)</math>, that switches the two factors.

** For a concrete example of this, let <math>V\cong\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2</math> be the [[Klein four-group]]. Since this group is [[abelian group|abelian]], every subgroup is normal; however, every permutation of the <math>3</math> non-identity elements is an automorphism of <math>V</math>, so the <math>3</math> subgroups of order <math>2</math> are not characteristic. Formally, <math>V=\{e,a,b,ab\}</math>. If <math>H=\{e,a\}</math> for example and <math>T</math> is the automorphism switching <math>a</math> and <math>b</math>, then <math>T(H)</math> is not contained in <math>H</math>.

* In the [[quaternion group]] of order 8, each of the cyclic subgroups of order 4 is normal, but none of these are characteristic.  However, the subgroup, <math>\{1,-1\}</math>, is characteristic, since it is the only subgroup of order 2.

* If <math>n>2</math> is even, the [[dihedral group]] of order <math>2n</math> has <math>3</math> subgroups of [[index of a subgroup|index]] <math>2</math>, all of which are normal.  One of these is the cyclic subgroup, which is characteristic.  The other two subgroups are dihedral; these are permuted by an [[outer automorphism group|outer automorphism]] of the parent group, and are therefore not characteristic.

===<span class="anchor" id="Strictly invariant subgroup"></span>Strictly characteristic subgroup===
A ''{{vanchor|strictly characteristic subgroup}}'', or a ''{{vanchor|distinguished subgroup}}'', is one which is invariant under [[surjective]] [[endomorphism]]s. For [[finite group]]s, surjectivity of an endomorphism implies injectivity, so a surjective endomorphism is an automorphism; thus, strictly characteristic is equivalent to characteristic. This is not the case for infinite groups.

===<span class="anchor" id="Fully invariant subgroup"></span>Fully characteristic subgroup===
For an even stronger constraint, a ''fully characteristic subgroup'' (also, ''fully invariant subgroup'') of a group <math>G</math>, is a subgroup ''H'' ≤ ''G'' that is invariant under every [[group homomorphism#Types|endomorphism]] of <math>G</math> (and not just every automorphism):
:{{math|∀φ ∈ End(''G'')： φ(''H'') ≤ ''H''}}.

Every group has itself (the improper subgroup) and the trivial subgroup as two of its fully characteristic subgroups. The [[commutator subgroup]] of a group is always a fully characteristic subgroup.{{sfnp|Scott|1964|pp=45–46}}{{sfnp|Magnus|Karrass|Solitar|2004|pp=74–85}}

Every endomorphism of <math>G</math> induces an endomorphism of <math>G/H</math>, which yields a map {{math|End(''G'') → End(''G''/''H'')}}.

=== Verbal subgroup ===
{{Main|Verbal subgroup}}
An even stronger constraint is [[verbal subgroup]], which is the image of a fully invariant subgroup of a [[free group]] under a homomorphism. More generally, any [[verbal subgroup]] is always fully characteristic. For any [[reduced free group]], and, in particular, for any [[free group]], the converse also holds: every fully characteristic subgroup is verbal.

== Transitivity ==
The property of being characteristic or fully characteristic is [[transitive relation|transitive]]; if <math>H</math> is a (fully) characteristic subgroup of <math>K</math>, and <math>K</math> is a (fully) characteristic subgroup of <math>G</math>, then <math>H</math> is a (fully) characteristic subgroup of <math>G</math>.
:{{math|''H'' char ''K'' char ''G'' ⇒ ''H'' char ''G''}}.

Moreover, while normality is not transitive, it is true that every characteristic subgroup of a normal subgroup is normal.
:{{math|''H'' char ''K'' ⊲ ''G'' ⇒ ''H'' ⊲ ''G''}}

Similarly, while being strictly characteristic (distinguished) is not transitive, it is true that every fully characteristic subgroup of a strictly characteristic subgroup is strictly characteristic.

However, unlike normality, if {{math|''H'' char ''G''}} and <math>K</math> is a subgroup of <math>G</math> containing <math>H</math>, then in general <math>H</math> is not necessarily characteristic in <math>K</math>.
:{{math|''H'' char ''G'', ''H'' < ''K'' < ''G'' ⇏ ''H'' char ''K''}}

== Containments ==
Every subgroup that is fully characteristic is certainly strictly characteristic and characteristic; but a characteristic or even strictly characteristic subgroup need not be fully characteristic.

The [[center of a group]] is always a strictly characteristic subgroup, but it is not always fully characteristic. For example, the finite group of order <math>12</math>, {{math|Sym(3) × <math>\Z/2 \Z</math>}}, has a homomorphism taking <math>(\pi,y)</math> to <math>((1,2)^y,0)</math>, which takes the center, <math>1 \times \Z/2\Z</math>, into a subgroup of {{math|Sym(3) × 1}}, which meets the center only in the identity.

The relationship amongst these subgroup properties can be expressed as:
:[[Normal subgroup|Normal]] ⇐ '''Characteristic''' ⇐ Strictly characteristic ⇐ [[Fully characteristic subgroup|Fully characteristic]] ⇐ [[Verbal subgroup|Verbal]]

==Examples==

=== Finite example ===
Consider the group <math>G = S_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_2</math> (the group of order 12 that is the direct product of the [[symmetric group]] of order 6 and a [[cyclic group]] of order 2). The center of <math>G</math> is isomorphic to its second factor <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math>. Note that the first factor, <math>S_3</math>, contains subgroups isomorphic to <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math>, for instance <math>{e, (12)}</math>; let <math>f: \mathbb{Z}_2 \rarr \text{S}_3</math> be the morphism mapping <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math> onto the indicated subgroup. Then the composition of the projection of <math>G</math> onto its second factor <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math>, followed by <math>f</math>, followed by the inclusion of <math>S_3</math> into <math>G</math> as its first factor, provides an endomorphism of <math>G</math> under which the image of the center, <math>\mathbb{Z}_2</math>, is not contained in the center, so here the center is not a fully characteristic subgroup of <math>G</math>.

=== Cyclic groups ===
Every subgroup of a cyclic group is characteristic.

=== Subgroup functors ===
The [[derived subgroup]] (or commutator subgroup) of a group is a verbal subgroup.  The [[torsion subgroup]] of an [[abelian group]] is a fully invariant subgroup.

=== Topological groups ===
The [[identity component]] of a [[topological group]] is always a characteristic subgroup.
